title: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
subtitle: Smith-Robinson approach, discectomy, cage and plate

sources.org: AO Spine / Cervical Spine Research Society, Fehlings MG et al. (Global Spine Journal)
sources.title: A clinical practice guideline for the management of patients with degenerative cervical myelopathy

sources.org: AANS/CNS Joint Section on Disorders of the Spine and Peripheral Nerves (J Neurosurg Spine)
sources.title: Guideline update for the performance of fusion procedures for degenerative disease of the lumbar spine

indications: Degenerative cervical myelopathy from disc or osteophyte compression at one or a few levels: surgery is recommended for moderate and severe myelopathy, and is an option for mild myelopathy (AO Spine guideline).
Cervical radiculopathy with concordant imaging, after failed non-operative treatment, or with progressive or significant motor weakness.
Disc-level compression where the pathology is anterior and the cervical alignment is lordotic or neutral.
contraindications: Compression mainly from behind (ligamentum flavum, multilevel congenital stenosis) or over many levels, which may suit a posterior approach.
Fixed kyphosis requiring a different reconstruction.
Active infection in the neck or the anterior cervical soft tissues; previous anterior neck surgery or radiotherapy needs ENT assessment of the vocal cords before operating on the opposite side.
Isolated axial neck pain without neural compression.
preparation: MRI reviewed for the level and the nature of compression; CT if ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament is suspected, because it changes the operation.
Record myelopathy and radiculopathy findings, and the mJOA score, as a baseline.
Pre-operative vocal cord assessment in patients with previous anterior neck surgery or a voice change.
Discuss intubation with the anaesthetist: a myelopathic patient needs the neck kept neutral, with video or awake fibreoptic intubation per their judgement.

Consent should include dysphagia (common, usually temporary), hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, neck haematoma with airway compromise, oesophageal or tracheal injury, dural tear, worsened myelopathy or root deficit (including C5 palsy), vertebral artery injury, non-union, implant problems, adjacent segment disease and wrong level.
positioning: Supine with a small roll between the shoulder blades and the neck in mild extension within the range the patient tolerated awake.
Shoulders gently taped down to allow a lateral image of the lower cervical spine, without traction injury to the brachial plexus.
Head on a ring, turned slightly away from the side of approach or kept neutral.
equipment: Self-retaining cervical retractor system and distraction pins.
Operating microscope or loupes and headlight.
High-speed drill with a fine burr, Kerrison rongeurs of small size, curettes, nerve hook.
Interbody cages and trials, graft material, anterior plate and screws.
anatomy: Surface landmarks: the hyoid lies at about C3, the thyroid cartilage at C4 and C5, the cricoid at C6; the carotid tubercle (Chassaignac) on C6. Image to confirm.
The approach passes between the carotid sheath laterally and the trachea and oesophagus medially, through the pretracheal fascia, to the prevertebral fascia and the longus colli.

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve runs a less predictable course around the subclavian artery, so many surgeons prefer a left-sided approach for low levels; the evidence on side and nerve injury is mixed.
The vertebral artery lies lateral to the uncovertebral joints in the transverse foramina; lateral drilling beyond the uncinate risks it.
The spinal cord lies directly behind the posterior longitudinal ligament; the exiting root runs through the foramen at the uncovertebral joint.
criticalSafety: Confirm the level with a needle and lateral image before any disc is opened.
Keep retractor blades under the longus colli, not on the oesophagus or carotid.
Work in the midline: identify the uncinate processes on each side and stay between them.
Do not pass instruments under the posterior longitudinal ligament with force; the cord has no room.
Neck haematoma after ACDF is an airway emergency: the plan for it is made before the patient leaves theatre.
structuresAtRisk: Carotid artery and internal jugular vein
Spinal cord and exiting nerve roots
Thoracic duct in low left-sided approaches
Sympathetic chain on the longus colli (Horner syndrome)
commonErrors: Wrong level from an inadequate image.
Retractor blades not seated under the longus colli, causing oesophageal pressure or injury.
Drilling off the midline towards the vertebral artery.
Inadequate decompression behind the vertebral body or in the foramen.
Plate placed over the adjacent disc, encouraging adjacent level ossification.
complications: Oesophageal perforation, sometimes presenting days later with fever and neck swelling.
Cord or root injury, including delayed C5 palsy.
Non-union, subsidence, implant failure; adjacent segment disease.
postop: Head up; observe the neck for swelling and the patient for stridor or difficulty swallowing. Keep a suture removal kit or clip remover at the bedside, per local policy.
Neurological observations: limb power, sensation and gait compared with the baseline.
Diet as swallowing allows; speech and language assessment if dysphagia is significant.
Erect lateral and AP radiographs per local practice.
Collar only if the surgeon asks for it.
New fever, neck swelling or pain on swallowing in the first days: suspect oesophageal injury.

steps.emphasis: Include dysphagia, hoarseness and the airway risk of a neck haematoma.
Record limb power, hand function, gait and the mJOA score; read the level from the MRI aloud.
Agree the intubation and neck position plan, monitoring, and the level and side of approach.
Supine, roll between the scapulae, gentle neck extension no further than tolerated awake, shoulders taped for imaging.
Check that the target level can be seen on a lateral view before preparing; large shoulders hide C6 and C7.
Skin marker before incision; a bent needle in the disc space after exposure, imaged before any disc is touched.
Baselines before any distraction or decompression in myelopathic patients.
Stay between the uncinate processes; remove the cartilage endplate without breaching the bony endplate.
Confirm cage height and footprint, and plate length, against the trials and the images.
Recess the cage behind the anterior vertebral margin and well in front of the posterior margin; release distraction before checking.
AP and lateral images showing the cage, the plate and the screw tips.
Release the retractors and inspect for bleeding from longus colli and the vertebral body edges; a neck haematoma is an airway emergency.
Close the platysma as a separate layer, then the skin; a drain is per surgeon preference.
Add the neck: swelling, stridor and swallowing, with the airway plan for a haematoma written down.

step.acdf.approach.title: Anterior approach to the cervical spine
step.acdf.approach.why: The anterior cervical approach uses a natural plane between the carotid sheath and the visceral column. Staying in that plane, with blunt dissection, protects the oesophagus, the carotid and the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
how: Make a transverse skin incision in a skin crease at the imaged level, from the midline to the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
Divide the platysma, then dissect bluntly along the medial border of sternocleidomastoid. Feel the carotid pulse and stay medial to it.
Open the pretracheal fascia and develop the plane between the carotid sheath laterally and the trachea and oesophagus medially, down to the prevertebral fascia.
Divide the prevertebral fascia in the midline and elevate the medial borders of both longus colli muscles with bipolar diathermy.
Seat the retractor blades under the longus colli on each side; some surgeons deflate and reinflate the endotracheal tube cuff after placing the retractor.
structuresAtRisk: Carotid artery and internal jugular vein
Superior thyroid and inferior thyroid vessels
pitfalls: Sharp dissection in the visceral plane.
Retractor blades placed on top of longus colli, slipping onto the oesophagus.
Dissecting lateral to longus colli and injuring the sympathetic chain.

step.acdf.decompression.title: Posterior osteophytes, posterior longitudinal ligament and foraminal decompression
step.acdf.decompression.why: In myelopathy and radiculopathy, the compression often lies behind the disc: osteophytes, disc fragments under or through the posterior longitudinal ligament, and uncovertebral spurs in the foramen. A discectomy that stops at the posterior annulus leaves the patient compressed.
how: Under magnification, thin the posterior osteophytes with a diamond burr, working parallel to the endplates.
Open the posterior longitudinal ligament with a hook and remove it with small Kerrison rongeurs when there is extruded disc behind it or the surgeon plans a complete decompression.
Decompress each foramen along the uncovertebral joint for radiculopathy, staying medial to the vertebral artery.
Confirm decompression by seeing the dura bulge forward and by passing a blunt hook into each foramen.
pitfalls: Pushing a Kerrison footplate under a ligament where the cord has no room.
Drilling laterally past the uncinate process.
Missing a sequestrated fragment behind the vertebral body.

step.acdf.plate.title: Anterior plate fixation
step.acdf.plate.why: A plate adds stability and reduces cage migration, particularly in multilevel constructs, but a plate that is too long overlaps the adjacent disc, and screws that are angled badly can enter the disc or the canal.
how: Remove anterior osteophytes so the plate lies flat on the vertebral bodies.
Choose the shortest plate that allows screws in each vertebral body without the plate reaching the adjacent discs.
Drill and insert screws at the angle the system specifies, with lateral images checking depth.
Lock the screws as the system requires and check that the plate does not overhang the adjacent disc.
pitfalls: An overlong plate encroaching on the adjacent disc.
A plate placed off the midline.
